content: Chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM), also known as chronic otitis media (COM), is a persistent condition characterized by inflammation and infection of the middle ear and mastoid cavity. This condition is typically associated with ear discharge (otorrhoea) through a perforated tympanic membrane, as well as hearing loss. One potential treatment for CSOM involves the use of topical antiseptics, which work by inhibiting the microorganisms responsible for the infection. These antiseptics can be used as a standalone treatment or in conjunction with other therapies, such as antibiotics or aural toileting (ear cleaning). However, the application of antiseptics may cause irritation to the skin of the outer ear, leading to symptoms such as discomfort, pain, or itching. Additionally, certain antiseptics, such as alcohol-based solutions, may pose a risk of ototoxicity, potentially resulting in sensorineural hearing loss, dizziness, or tinnitus. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of topical antiseptics in individuals with CSOM. A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane ENT Register, CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ICTRP, to identify relevant published and unpublished randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The search was completed on April 1, 2019. The inclusion criteria for the analysis were RCTs with a minimum follow-up period of one week, involving adults or children with chronic ear discharge of unknown cause or CSOM lasting more than two weeks. The interventions studied included any single or combination of topical antiseptic agents, administered directly into the ear canal as drops, powders, or irrigations, or as part of an aural toileting procedure. The comparisons included: (a) topical antiseptics versus placebo or no intervention, and (b) one topical antiseptic versus another. Studies were further categorized based on whether both groups received antiseptics alone or with aural toileting, or in addition to antibiotic treatment. The analysis followed standard Cochrane methodological procedures, and the GRADE system was used to assess the certainty of the evidence for each outcome. The primary outcomes of interest were the resolution of ear discharge (or achieving a dry ear), health-related quality of life, and ear pain or local irritation. Secondary outcomes included hearing, serious complications, and ototoxicity. Five studies were included in the review. However, the total number of participants could not be determined because two studies only reported the number of ears included. 1. Topical antiseptic (boric acid) versus placebo or no treatment (all patients underwent aural toileting): Three studies compared topical antiseptics with no treatment, but only one study (a cluster-RCT involving 254 children) provided usable data. This study compared boric acid in alcohol ear drops with no ear drops, with both groups performing daily dry mopping for one month. Adjustments were made to account for intra-cluster correlation. The evidence, rated as very low certainty, suggests it is unclear whether boric acid treatment increases the resolution of ear discharge at four weeks (risk ratio [RR] 1.94, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.20 to 3.16; 174 participants) or at three to four months (RR 1.73, 95% CI 1.21 to 2.47; 180 participants). The study narratively reported no differences in suspected ototoxicity or hearing outcomes between the treatment arms. None of the studies reported on health-related quality of life, adverse effects, or serious complications. 2. Topical antiseptic A versus topical antiseptic B: Two studies compared different antiseptics, but only one study (93 participants) provided data for this comparison. This study compared a single application of boric acid powder with daily acetic acid ear drops. The evidence, rated as very low certainty, suggests it is uncertain whether boric acid powder leads to a higher resolution of ear discharge at four weeks (RR 2.61, 95% CI 1.51 to 4.53; 93 participants). Similarly, it is unclear whether there is a difference in ear discomfort between the two treatments due to the low number of reported events (RR 0.10, 95% CI 0.01 to 1.81; 93 participants). The study narratively reported no differences in hearing outcomes between the groups. None of the included studies reported on other primary or secondary outcomes. In conclusion, the evidence regarding the effectiveness and safety of topical antiseptics for the treatment of CSOM is limited and of very low certainty. As a result, the efficacy and safety profile of these treatments remain uncertain.
